nodes.title: Amazon S3: Key Ideas
nodes.content: S3 is AWS's object store — flat namespace of buckets containing objects, accessed via HTTP. It backs almost every AWS architecture: data lakes, static sites, backups, lambda triggers, CloudFront origins. The exam tests storage classes, encryption, access control, and event notifications.

flashcards.front: S3 storage classes — pick one for backups, one for hot data, one for archive.
flashcards.back: Hot: S3 Standard (high cost, instant access). Backups / infrequent: S3 Standard-IA (cheaper storage, retrieval fee). Archive: Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest storage, retrieval in hours). Lifecycle policies move objects between classes automatically based on age.

flashcards.front: S3 bucket policy vs IAM policy vs ACL — which to use?
flashcards.back: IAM policy: 'this user/role can read bucket X'. Bucket policy: 'these principals can access this bucket' — required for cross-account and public access. ACL (legacy): per-object permissions, mostly avoided today. Use bucket policies for most cross-account, IAM for in-account.

flashcards.front: How do you make an S3 website (static-site hosting)?
flashcards.back: Enable static-website hosting on the bucket, upload index.html, set a bucket policy allowing public-read on objects, point a CloudFront distribution at it for HTTPS + edge caching. Don't expose the bucket directly — CloudFront with an OAC (Origin Access Control) is the canonical pattern.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between server-side and client-side encryption?
flashcards.back: SSE: data encrypted by S3 after upload. Variants: SSE-S3 (AWS-managed key, easiest), SSE-KMS (your KMS key, audit trail), SSE-C (you supply the key on each request). Client-side: you encrypt before upload — S3 only sees ciphertext. Pick SSE-KMS for compliance, SSE-S3 for default-on.

questions.q: A security engineer needs to ensure all data stored in an S3 bucket is encrypted with a specific CMK, and any PutObject request without SSE-KMS using that key is rejected. How should the bucket policy be written?
choices: Enable default bucket encryption with SSE-KMS and the CMK — this automatically rejects non-KMS uploads
Create a KMS key policy that only allows encryption for objects uploaded to the specific S3 bucket
Create a bucket policy allowing all s3:PutObject actions and trust KMS to enforce encryption
Create a bucket policy with a Deny on s3:PutObject where s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption is not 'aws:kms' AND
questions.explanation: A bucket policy with a Deny condition checks the PutObject request headers. The condition 'StringNotEquals: s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption: aws:kms' denies uploads not using SSE-KMS. Adding 'StringNotEquals: s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id: <key-ARN>' further enforces that only the specific CMK is used. Default encryption applies KMS if no header is provided but doesn't reject non-compliant requests — the bucket policy Deny is needed for strict enforcement.

questions.q: A developer needs read access to an S3 bucket in Account B from an EC2 instance in Account A. The bucket policy in Account B already grants s3:GetObject to Account A's EC2 role ARN. However, the GetObject calls are still failing. What is the MOST likely missing configuration?
choices: The bucket in Account B must have versioning enabled for cross-account access
The EC2 instance's IAM role in Account A must also have an identity-based policy granting
Account A must create a VPC endpoint for S3 to enable cross-account bucket access
Account B must have VPC peering with Account A for S3 cross-account access
questions.explanation: Cross-account S3 access requires BOTH policies to allow: (1) The bucket policy in Account B must grant access to Account A's IAM role, AND (2) The IAM role in Account A must have an identity-based policy allowing s3:GetObject on the specific bucket ARN in Account B. This is different from same-account access where a bucket policy alone can grant access. If either policy denies or doesn't allow, the access fails.

questions.q: A company needs to enforce that all S3 buckets created in their accounts use SSE-KMS encryption and have public access blocked. New accounts joining the organization must automatically comply. Which combination achieves this with ZERO manual per-account configuration?
choices: Create Lambda functions in each account triggered by S3 bucket creation events to enforce the settings
Apply an SCP denying s3:CreateBucket without SSE-KMS headers;.
Create a CloudFormation StackSet that deploys S3 bucket policies to all accounts on creation
Use AWS Control Tower to set detective guardrails checking S3 encryption and Block Public Access settings
questions.explanation: S3 Block Public Access can now be enabled at the AWS Organizations level, automatically applying to all existing and new accounts. An SCP can deny S3 bucket creation without the SSE-KMS header, preventing creation of unencrypted buckets. Config conformance packs deployed via StackSets with automatic deployment cover new accounts automatically. Together these create a zero-touch enforcement layer for all current and future accounts. enable S3 Block Public Access at the organization level via Amazon S3 account settings in Organizations; configure AWS Config conformance packs via StackSets with automatic deployment

questions.q: A bucket policy denies all requests where aws:SecureTransport is false. Which TWO additional controls would you add to BLOCK accidental public exposure of objects in this bucket?
choices: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the bucket level
Enable default S3 server-side encryption with SSE-S3
Enable S3 Object Ownership set to "Bucket owner enforced" (disables ACLs)
questions.explanation: Block Public Access overrides any policy/ACL that would grant Public access. "Bucket owner enforced" disables ACLs entirely so an uploader can't accidentally make an individual object public. SSE-S3 protects data at rest but not against public exposure. MFA Delete protects against accidental deletion of versions, not against public reads.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
